section_title: Why are the people told to rejoice when the Law has moved them to tears?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 9 Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were instructing the people said to all of them, “This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep.” For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law. 10 Then Nehemiah told them, “Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared, since today is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.” 11 And the Levites calmed all the people, saying, “Be still, since today is holy. Do not grieve.” 12 Then all the people began to eat and drink, to send out portions, and to rejoice greatly, because they understood the words that had been made known to them.

context_lines: The people weep as they hear the Law, but Nehemiah, Ezra and the teaching Levites tell them that this day is holy to God and should be celebrated. [Leviticus 23:23–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/leviticus/23.htm) identifies the first day of the seventh month as a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts.
Nehemiah sends them to enjoy a meal and share portions with those who have nothing prepared. Their celebration is to include people who would otherwise go without.

The people leave rejoicing because they have understood the words explained to them. Their tears are followed by a welcome to find strength in joy before God; confession will receive its own place later in the month.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/nehemiah/8.htm) sees the tears as evidence of tender hearts and stresses the generosity that should accompany the feast. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm) understands joy directed toward God and received from Him as renewing the people’s strength to serve. Neither treats the call to rejoice on this holy day as a denial that sin needs to be confessed.
god_plan_lines: The movement from sorrow to joy has a wider biblical parallel. [Zechariah 12:10–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/zechariah/12.htm) describes mourning over the pierced One, and [John 19:34–37](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/19.htm) connects the pierced One with Jesus’ crucifixion.

Jesus also tells His disciples that their grief will turn to joy when they see Him again ([John 16:16–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/16.htm)). These are parallels in the way God brings people through sorrow into joy, rather than a statement that Nehemiah’s gathering is itself a prediction of those events. The New Testament grounds that lasting joy in Christ.
